section_summary: This section documents the mounting difficulties encountered by American motion picture distributors in Japan between 1938 and early 1940 due to stringent Japanese exchange control laws, import quotas, and the comprehensive regulatory regime established by the 1939 Motion Picture Law. It details the 1938 agreement permitting limited film imports and a three-year deferred remittance of three million yen in royalties, subsequent restrictions halting import permits and reducing quotas to 120 foreign films, and the accumulation of four million yen in frozen American funds. Following urgent appeals from the Motion Picture Producers and Distributors of America and local distributors, the Department of State instructed Ambassador Joseph C. Grew in Tokyo to make representations to the Japanese Foreign Office seeking an expansion of the American film quota and the unfreezing of commercial revenues.

subfiles.summary: Kojiro Nakamura of the Japanese Department of Finance outlines the conditions for approving the importation of American motion pictures under credit based on the May 28, 1938 application by Hisaji Kubo. American companies are permitted to import up to $30,000 in print costs at a minimum rate of 1.5 cents per foot before the end of 1938, subject to monthly approval and ideological vetting. Earned royalties up to 3,000,000 yen may be remitted through the Yokohama Specie Bank and held without interest in its San Francisco branch for three years before disbursement. Annexed documents include an outline of the memorandum submitted by the American Motion Picture Association of Japan requesting remittance and raw film supplies, as well as extracts of relevant foreign exchange control ordinances from 1933 and 1937.

subfiles.from: Ministries of Home Affairs, Education, and Welfare
subfiles.summary: This official translation of Joint Ministerial Ordinance No. 1 details the administrative regulations enforcing Japan's Motion Picture Law of 1939. It prescribes application and permit procedures for motion picture production and distribution, mandatory annual reports, and vocational registration for directors, actors, and cameramen. The ordinance establishes a quota system under the Home Minister limiting foreign dramatic films, defines censorship disqualification criteria for domestic exhibition and export, restricts theater exhibition hours to three hours, limits theaters to fifty foreign feature prints annually, and bars children under fourteen from unapproved screenings.
subfiles.title: The Regulations Concerning the Enforcement of the Motion Picture Law (Joint Ministerial Ordinance No. 1)

subfiles.about: Comprehensive consular report on the Motion Picture Law of Japan, accompanying ordinances, import quotas, film releases, taxation, and market conditions.
subfiles.from: C. R. Cameron, American Consul General, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Consul General C. R. Cameron submits a comprehensive voluntary report examining the promulgation and economic impact of Joint Ministerial Ordinance No. 1 and related Imperial Ordinances enforcing Japan's Motion Picture Law. The report reviews the history of the 1938 remittance agreement, provides detailed statistics on foreign film releases from 1935 through November 1939, and analyzes the 1940 import applications, predicting an overall cap of 100 foreign films. Cameron details program limits of three hours, the annual 50-print ceiling per theater, overlapping censorship by the Home and Education Ministries, the corporate feud between Toho and Shochiku over Nikkatsu stock, and confidential matters including defective Fuji raw film, arbitrary taxation by the Kanda-bashi office, and an increasingly pessimistic commercial outlook for American distributors.
subfiles.title: Consular Report No. 74: 'New Regulations for Motion Pictures in Japan'

subfiles.about: Unofficial translation of Joint Ministerial Ordinance No. 1 enforcing Japan's Motion Picture Law, setting rules on business permits, personnel registration, foreign film quotas, and censorship.
subfiles.from: Ministries of Home Affairs, Education, and Welfare
subfiles.summary: This enclosure transmits an unofficial English translation prepared by a local translating bureau of Joint Ministerial Ordinance No. 1, promulgated on September 26, 1939. The regulations prescribe detailed requirements for obtaining production and distribution licenses, filing annual operational reports, registering creative personnel, and restricting the working hours of minors and female employees. The document also defines foreign films, establishes an annual distribution quota for foreign dramatic features under the jurisdiction of the Home Minister, and outlines standards for export and domestic censorship, with the text breaking off during Article 27.
subfiles.title: Enclosure No. 1 to Report No. 74: 'Translation of Joint Ministerial Ordinance No. 1... Motion Picture Law Enforcement Regulations'
